Large language models are widely used as judges of model outputs (LLM-as-a-Judge), but they are costly and can hallucinate or be overconfident. Decision models are a potential alternative. They return a predefined verdict with a probability for each label instead of free-form text and are much cheaper and faster. We test this promise on hallucination detection. We build binary benchmarks for five hallucination types (9,852 items from six datasets) and compare five decision models with the generative judge gpt-6-sol. Performance depends strongly on the type: the best decision model matches gpt-6-sol in balanced accuracy on context inconsistency and comes within 3 percentage points on factual errors, but trails it by 4-8 points on logical and instruction inconsistency. Decision-model probabilities are overconfident, though less so than the GPT-6 models, and separate correct from incorrect decisions only moderately. We also find that a confidence cascade of decision models improves on the best single model by 1.9-3.3 points on three types and matches or exceeds gpt-6-sol at 1-3% of its cost. Overall, decision models are a practical low-cost judge for some hallucination types but need to be validated before use.

World models are widely proposed as core components for enabling agents to reason over long temporal and spatial horizons. Yet current evaluations often emphasize task performance while providing limited insight into whether learned world models acquire predictive latent dynamics that reflect the underlying structure of the environment. Here we introduce the concept of faithful latent world models as an equivariance condition between the environment's transition map and the learned latent dynamics. We propose latent rollout consistency (LRC) as a metric to evaluate action-conditioned latent prediction. Strikingly, we find that across the studied state of the art latent world models, none solves the task by actually faithfully modeling the dynamics of the environment.

To be socially sustainable, Agentic AI systems require normative designs that align responsibilities with the ability to fulfil them. Identifying incongruences such as unsatisfiable expectations or privilege escalation is crucial in avoiding normative pitfalls. In this study, we discuss design dimensions suitable for describing multi-agent systems in light of this norm-ability alignment requirement. We propose a formal framework centred on process-oriented modelling and institutional power for the analysis of a given normatively relevant process, discuss strategies for repairing it, and elaborate on how the symmetrical relation between operational process and institutional state affects the lifecycle of normative positions.

Recent advances in interactive world models have made it possible to generate controllable, dynamic environments from action inputs. Yet current models struggle to maintain coherence beyond roughly one minute of rollout, a limitation rooted not in model capacity but in the scarcity of long-horizon training data. Existing gameplay video datasets typically consist of clips under ten seconds, with captions that describe whole clips in coarse and undifferentiated text, which is insufficient for controllable long-horizon generation. We address this with GameVerse, a minute-scale gameplay video dataset purpose-built for long-horizon interactive world modeling. GameVerse contains 69.7K clips spanning 1,655 hours and 349.6 million frames across diverse first- and third-person gameplay, including 1,358 hours of continuous two-minute sequences, an order of magnitude longer than prior datasets. Clips pass through a unified pipeline of scene-consistent segmentation, quality filtering, camera pose estimation, and event-based caption annotation. Each clip is paired with a temporally stable camera trajectory that remains coherent across minutes, together with captions that separate static scene context from dynamic foreground events and align to event boundaries rather than fixed time windows. Comprehensive analysis shows that GameVerse surpasses existing public datasets in scale, diversity, and annotation quality. Experiments further demonstrate that training on GameVerse substantially extends the temporal horizon of interactive world models.

In this work, we propose Subspace Clifford Networks, a reformulation that replaces global cyclic rolling with grouped subspace interactions. Instead of sampling sparse cyclic diagonals across the entire $D$-dimensional channel space, we project the features into an aligned space $\R^{\tilde{D}} = \bigoplus_{g=1}^{G} V_g$ partitioned into $G$ low-dimensional groups $V_g \cong \R^k$ with $k \in \{2, 3, 4\}$. Within each $k$-dimensional group, we compute all $\binom{k}{2}$ wedge coordinates and concatenate them with $\operatorname{SiLU}$-activated coordinate-wise products, while sandwiching the grouped interaction between learnable $1\times 1$ linear projections to enable cross-group channel mixing. This design reduces intermediate feature expansion from $2|\mathcal{S}|D$ (typically $10D$ for 5 shifts) down to $1.5\tilde{D}$ ($k=2$), $2.0\tilde{D}$ ($k=3$), or $2.5\tilde{D}$ ($k=4$). Furthermore, exploiting the small, fixed group size $k \in \{2, 3, 4\}$, we implement a fused CUDA kernel that evaluates the forward interaction and a recomputation-based analytical backward pass using thread-local variables without allocating global-memory buffers for elementwise intermediates. Finally, we extend the backbone from an isotropic columnar layout to a multi-resolution Hierarchical Clifford Network with configurable per-stage subspace dimensions. Experiments on CIFAR-100 show that the proposed models substantially reduce parameter count and training time across both regimes, while the hierarchical variants also improve classification accuracy over the evaluated shift-based hierarchical baselines.

Fine-grained visual perception remains a bottleneck during post-training of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), as perceptual errors can constrain gains from reasoning-focused optimization. Although image-caption pre-training improves perception, its influence can weaken as subsequent stages change data mixtures and objectives. Continuing caption supervision during post-training is challenging because subjective, information-dense descriptions complicate verifiable reward design. We present PerceptRL, which strengthens perception at two complementary levels. Perception RL uses a multi-agent pipeline to extract verified errors from dense image captions and convert the corresponding visual facts into QA pairs with fixed answer labels and rule-based rewards. Chain QA links correlated errors, while multiple-choice QA combines unrelated errors. A specialized route targets high-error domains with tailored verification, and a domain-agnostic general route covers errors beyond these domains. Perception Agentic RL addresses fine-grained and dense cases unresolved by single-turn Perception RL through multi-turn inspection with visual tools. We observe coordinate drift even in models trained to use tools, where incorrect crops or annotations distort evidence and propagate errors. Coordinate Injection corrects spatial operations in cold-start trajectories, while a grounding-aware process reward supervises intermediate spatial fidelity alongside final-answer correctness. Training proceeds through shared cold-start SFT, single-turn Perception RL, and multi-turn Perception Agentic RL. Across seven benchmarks under a shared tool-use protocol, PerceptRL achieves 71.6% average accuracy, surpassing the base model with the same tools and the strongest evaluated frontier VLM by 15.7 and 5.2 percentage points, respectively.

Visual generation requires both high-level semantic knowledge and fine-grained pixel details. We propose a learning paradigm that assigns these roles to autoregressive pretraining for knowledge acquisition and diffusion post-training for high-fidelity rendering. Within this framework, we study the objective, representation, and scaling of knowledge acquisition and rendering. Controlled comparisons identify autoregression as the stronger pretraining objective for downstream rendering, improving both learning efficiency and final generation quality. We further find that AR-only generation quality does not necessarily correlate with final performance; semantic quality matters more. This motivates a purely semantic tokenizer trained with language supervision alone, without an image decoder or reconstruction loss. We establish compute-optimal scaling laws for knowledge acquisition and rendering, and find that autoregressive pretraining lowers the fitted asymptotic rendering loss compared with pixel diffusion models trained from scratch. Guided by the laws, we train a 3B-parameter text-to-image model with only 6,600 H100 GPU-hours, achieving 86 on GenEval and 87 on DPG-Bench and validating the proposed paradigm at scale.

Existing evaluations of text-conditioned 3D indoor scene generation largely emphasize semantic fidelity and physical validity at rest, leaving interaction-time physical reliability insufficiently assessed. To address this gap, we introduce ScIntBench, a unified benchmark centered on interaction readiness: it executes prescribed manipulation actions (e.g., pushing, opening, and surface probing) in physics simulation and measures task success, capability and progress, post-interaction integrity, and dynamic plausibility. Multi-view semantic and static physical evaluations complement these metrics and help explain interaction outcomes. We systematically evaluate 12 state-of-the-art scene generation systems across 10 room types. Our results reveal that strong semantic and static physical performance does not necessarily translate into interaction readiness: a system with near-perfect static plausibility completes only 11.54% of interactions, 7 of the 12 systems produce scenes that cannot support any interaction, and even the best system succeeds in only 36.92% of prescribed tasks. These findings highlight two fundamental challenges in generating interaction-ready scenes: providing the necessary physical interaction capabilities and ensuring reliable physical behavior under active manipulation.

Face swapping transfers a source identity onto a target image while preserving the target's pose, expression, hair, and lighting. The most realistic current methods are diffusion-based, but they need many network evaluations per image. GAN-based methods are fast, yet trained from scratch they must learn realism from the adversarial signal alone and produce visibly weaker results. We present ALADDIN (Adversarial Latent Diffusion Distillation for One-Step Identity Swapping), a one-step face swapper obtained by initialising the generator from a pre-trained multi-step flow-matching model and training it adversarially under identity and target-preservation constraints. We expose a controllable trade-off between identity transfer and target-attribute preservation by training a student model with triplet pseudo-label supervision. We additionally identify a bias in the standard evaluation protocol, which favours methods trained against the same identity encoder used to score them, and re-evaluate all baselines with an independent one. ALADDIN is state-of-the-art among one-step methods in realism and target preservation at comparable identity transfer, and matches the best multi-step model with 28 times fewer network evaluations and an order of magnitude fewer training samples.

Visual world models increasingly support spatial reasoning by generating RGB views of unobserved states. However, RGB has become the default interface largely because it is well suited for visual generation, rather than necessarily being the most effective representation for downstream reasoning. Different spatial questions may benefit from different representations of the same imagined state: top-down geometry can facilitate global distance comparisons, while panoramic views provide broader context for reasoning about open space. To isolate the role of representation in spatial imagination, we introduce ImagiRep, a simulator-grounded benchmark of 922 questions spanning seven question types across two settings, Viewpoint Imagination and Cross-view Integration, providing oracle RGB and six alternative representations (e.g., depth, panoramic views, and top-down geometry) of the same unobserved state. This controlled comparison reveals that even accurate imagined RGB does not guarantee accurate spatial reasoning, and different questions benefit from different representations. Similar trends hold for representations derived from world-model-estimated states. Notably, estimated RGB alone can mislead spatial reasoning, while alternative representations retain complementary benefits. Building on these findings, we introduce GEARS, a lightweight test-time strategy for adaptive representation selection, outperforming existing spatial imagination methods and showing that reasoning about unseen states requires more than generating RGB views.

Threading a quadrotor through a moving narrow gap is a demanding test of agile flight, requiring centimeter-level spatial alignment and precise temporal execution. We address this challenge using a control policy that operates directly on onboard visual and inertial measurements to output collective thrust and body-rate commands. The task is difficult because success lies on a thin feasible manifold: small errors in timing, position, attitude, or visual observability cause collision. Prior planning and learning methods rely on privileged state, teachers, planners, or distillation; learning dynamic narrow-gap traversal directly, from scratch, remains open. We introduce a differentiable moving-gap formulation that gates centering, alignment, and smooth collision terms by signed distance to a time-varying gap plane, turning a sparse traversal event into a dense pathwise objective. We integrate this formulation into a visual-feature-to-command policy trained in one stage from random initialization, without a teacher, planner, or distillation. We validate our approach in both synthetic and real-world experiments. In controlled benchmarks, we demonstrate that pathwise gradients significantly outperform score-function gradients for precision-critical tasks, yielding a 99.3% success rate in simulation after only a few minutes of training on a single GPU. Furthermore, the policy transfers directly to a real quadrotor, successfully crossing a dynamic narrow gap from varied initial conditions using onboard sensing and inertial measurements, achieving an 80% success rate over 10 physical trials.

Films introduce characters incrementally as they progress. We study the problem of identifying principal characters and assigning their names directly from the movie itself, without using external cast lists, actor photographs, or pre-built character banks. We introduce the character naming task: given a name mentioned in dialogue and the associated video context, the model must determine which visible character bears that name. This task is challenging because name resolution often depends on cinematic cues such as shot-reverse-shot structure, self-introduction, direct address, third-party reference, gaze, and temporal continuity. We provide a dataset and annotations for evaluating character naming and first character appearances, develop a video-and-dialogue model for the task, and compare it with proprietary multimodal large language models. We further introduce a progressive framework for building a character bank as the film unfolds. Together, these contributions support online, human-like movie understanding in which character identities are inferred from the film itself.

Rocky planets the size of Earth or larger are expected to undergo one or more giant impacts during the final stages of their formation. Some of these collisions occur after protoplanetary disk dissipation, potentially driving the loss of primordial hydrogen-rich atmospheres through elevated surface temperatures. However, whether giant impacts promote atmospheric loss or retention remains unclear because they both heat planetary interiors and increase atmospheric gravitational binding. Here we model the evolution of rocky planets after their largest post-disk giant impact, accounting self-consistently for the concurrent increase in gravitational binding energy and mantle thermal energy. Whereas the entire accreted mass contributes to the increase in gravitational binding energy, only part of the impact energy raises mantle temperature. Mantle melting consumes energy as latent heat, while the impactor's metallic core transfers little energy to the mantle and remains superheated at depth. Giant impacts therefore increase gravitational binding energy more than mantle thermal energy, shifting planets towards atmospheric retention. Larger, atmosphere-bearing planets emerge preferentially through collisional growth. By contrast, smaller planets without such impacts tend to lose their primordial atmospheres under sustained stellar irradiation. At the population level, these results suggest that sub-Neptunes have, on average, more massive rocky interiors than super-Earths.

Discrete visual tokens represent vision in a discrete form analogous to language, offering a native interface for multimodal modeling under a shared next-token prediction objective. However, quantization error is widely assumed to cause unavoidable semantic loss, fundamentally limiting the semantic fidelity of discrete visual tokens and positioning continuous visual representations as an intrinsic upper bound. Using multimodal understanding as a proxy for semantic fidelity, we revisit this assumption and find quantization error unreliable, as discrete representations with substantially larger errors can achieve better understanding. Instead, the effective bit budget of discrete indices emerges as a key determinant of downstream performance. However, existing quantizers eventually saturate as additional codebooks contribute progressively less semantic information. As one approach to alleviating this saturation, we introduce Factorized Vector Quantization, which quantizes complementary, fixed-dimensional views of the visual feature with symmetric parallel codebooks. It continues to improve at larger bit budgets, ultimately matching continuous visual representations in multimodal understanding. Trained on industrial-scale multimodal data, our model achieves state-of-the-art performance among discrete-representation models, outperforming UniAR and Emu3-Chat by 22.8% and 59.2%, respectively, on a nine-metric average. To our knowledge, it is also the first discrete-representation model competitive with strong continuous-representation models such as Qwen3-VL, including on fine-grained OCR tasks. We further identify the key principles and a practical recipe enabling this competitiveness. These results and insights support the potential of discrete visual representations to underpin large-scale native multimodal foundation models. Code and models are available at https://github.com/hustvl/FVQ

Rotating black holes offer powerful probes of gravity, but constructing their geometries beyond vacuum general relativity remains challenging. Here we develop a unified framework for constructing stationary, axisymmetric deformations of Kerr from their tidal curvature and physical sources. As a demonstration, we obtain closed-form solutions for six higher-curvature interactions at leading order in the couplings and for generic subextremal spin, without slow-rotation expansions, numerical fitting, or mode decomposition. The solutions pass stringent checks against the field equations, previous mode-by-mode constructions, and known analytic predictions for horizon quantities. We find that the chirality of the interactions organizes the analytic structure of these solutions, a pattern that likely extends to a large class of purely metric higher-curvature theories. Our framework opens a systematic route to black-hole geometries in beyond-Einstein theories and perturbative astrophysical environments. These geometries provide a foundation for strong-field tests with gravitational waves and other observational channels, such as black-hole images and X-ray spectroscopy, as well as theoretical studies of near-extremal black holes.

Generative models support content creation across text, images, videos, and design disciplines, yet their interfaces rely primarily on natural language. While effective for specifying high-level intent, language can be inefficient and imprecise for fine-grained control, iterative refinement, and open-ended exploration. We present PolyGandr, a visual interface for exploring relationships between latent representations and generated outputs, complementing natural-language model steering. PolyGandr formulates generative control as high-dimensional navigation, enabling users to define starting points, steering directions, and step sizes through a unified map-and-mixing-palette interface. Combining global exploration with local refinement supports both broad design-space navigation and fine-grained output manipulation without repeatedly translating visual intent into prompts. We evaluate PolyGandr across three use cases: StyleGAN2 face generation, Stable Diffusion chair design, and rotational kirigami engineering. A formative study indicates that PolyGandr complements existing workflows by supporting real-time editing while simultaneously providing an overview and means to explore the broader design space.

We present RESPLE2, a recursive multi-sensor state estimation framework using non-uniform B-splines for 6-DoF motion representation. By exploiting the knot-clamping boundary property, we propose a theoretically grounded mechanism for exact control-point prediction directly informed by inertial kinematics along the trajectory, with knot placement adapted to motion and measurement availability. Within an iterated extended Kalman filter, we perform this prediction using a subset of inertial measurements. A subsequent reset step preserves trajectory consistency as the knots extend. The update step further incorporates heterogeneous sensor measurements at their native timestamps through continuous-time observation models, supporting flexible combinations of LiDARs, cameras, inertial measurement units, and leg kinematics. We further develop a lightweight global optimization module that directly refines non-uniform B-spline control points by incorporating loop-closure constraints derived from LiDAR-visual cues. We conduct extensive evaluations on public and experimental datasets across handheld, tracked, legged, and hybrid aerial-legged platforms, covering highly dynamic maneuvers with extreme accelerations. Compared with state-of-the-art multi-sensor odometry systems, RESPLE2 achieves competitive or superior estimation accuracy and robustness in the corresponding sensor configurations, particularly under aggressive motion, while maintaining real-time operation. We publicly release our code and experimental datasets at https://github.com/ASIG-X/RESPLE2.

Video captioning aims to preserve visual information through compact descriptions, predominantly using natural language. However, precisely expressing fine-grained spatial structures and temporal dynamics in natural language often leads to lengthy and potentially ambiguous descriptions. In this work, we explore Code as Video Caption, a paradigm where executable programs serve as a complementary representation of visual content through graphical primitives, layout rules, and functions of time. To examine whether code captions effectively preserve video information, we compare them with natural language captions on downstream question answering and video reconstruction tasks. Our results show that code captions achieve superior reasoning accuracy and reconstruction fidelity. Despite these advantages, realizing the potential of code captioning depends on whether current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can generate faithful code captions. To systematically assess this capability, we introduce CodeCap-Bench, which comprises 323 videos spanning five categories of structured 2D content, along with fine-grained annotations and a multi-level evaluation framework. Extensive experiments reveal that while leading proprietary MLLMs demonstrate promising code captioning capabilities, they still struggle to faithfully capture complex temporal dynamics, with open-source models lagging substantially behind.

What is the intrinsic reason of emergence of macroscopic order parameter out of microscopic systems? In this article, we apply to physics the collective predictive coding (CPC), the theory of language/symbol emergence. As our language emerges out of our human communications, physical macroscopic order parameter emerges out of communications among atoms --- each atom is regarded as an agent who predicts each other's behavior through inference. We present three examples of classical spin systems: two-dimensional ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, a two-dimensional spin model with competing stripe orders, and the fully connected Sherrington--Kirkpatrick spin-glass model. In all of these examples, proper macroscopic order parameters including the replica overlap emerge automatically through communication informatics of CPC, only from observed spin configurations. We call the learned macroscopic coordinate the collective predictive order. Furthermore, for the ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic Ising models, the equilibrium distribution of the collective predictive order yields an emergent potential with the symmetry and thermal evolution characteristic of a Landau potential. Notably, the emergence of the collective predictive order does not refer to any structure of microscopic Hamiltonians/Lagrangians. Thus our ``Atom-as-an-Agent" (AaaA) principle offers a completely data-driven method for the emergence of macroscopic order, that is, machine learning physics.

We propose a test of whether two interventions induce the same outcome distribution when outcomes are structured and high-dimensional, such as images, text and graphs. We represent the interventional distributions as mean embeddings on learned deep features, such that the treatment effect is a doubly robust representation of the difference in mean embeddings. Our test, DR-KTE-Deep, optimises the learned features so as to maximise an estimated power criterion on this treatment effect representation. To motivate our learning objective, we show that the power criterion characterises the asymptotic signal-to-noise ratio of the test under fixed alternatives, and we derive a uniform finite-sample bound for its regularised estimate. We show that, with the learned kernel fixed, a held-out test is asymptotically valid under the null given suitable nuisance-estimation rates. Empirically, DR-KTE-Deep achieves substantially higher power than fixed and bandwidth-optimised kernel baselines across image, text and graph outcomes, while maintaining well-calibrated Type-I error.

JWST surveys find more UV-bright galaxies at $z>10$ than galaxy-formation models predict, but the roles of recent star formation, stellar mass and dust remain uncertain. We analyse 1365 spectroscopically confirmed JADES galaxies at $3\leq z\leq9$, fitting NIRCam photometry and NIRSpec emission lines with \ceri. Our model includes flexible star-formation histories (SFHs) under three priors, two-component dust attenuation and nebular emission. We account for spectroscopic selection through population reweighting and assess the reliability of inferred trends. At $z=3$--5, rising SFHs are more common in low-mass galaxies, whereas most galaxies above $10^{9.5}\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$ have declining SFHs. The apparent increase in rising fractions with redshift cannot be distinguished from the adopted SFH prior alone. At fixed stellar mass, recent star formation is the strongest predictor of UV brightness. UV-brighter galaxies have higher recent SFRs, younger stellar populations and less attenuation at fixed SFR. Below $10^9\,{\rm M}_{\odot}$, they are also more likely to have rising SFHs, with odds increasing by up to a factor of 2.3 per magnitude brighter, although the strongest trend requires caution. In contrast, galaxies with $M_{\mathrm{UV}}<-20$ at $z=3$--5 are predominantly massive, and approximately half have declining SFHs. Dust partly offsets burst-driven UV brightening: attenuation increases with recent SFR and declines gradually after the inferred SFR peak. In model sensitivity tests, dust has the largest effect on bright-end counts, whereas removing galaxy-to-galaxy SFH scatter changes them by at most 0.17~dex. Thus, bursts can make low-mass galaxies unusually UV-bright for their mass, while the absolute bright end of the UVLF is primarily shaped by stellar mass and dust attenuation.

This Letter investigates gravitational-wave tests of the horizon area law. Although they provide a striking consistency check of general relativity (GR), these tests rely on models that assume GR, making their interpretation inherently model dependent. We show with a specific example---simulations of merging boson stars---that exotic compact objects can mimic merging black holes and pass an area-law test at a confidence as high as $\sim 92\%$ despite not even having event horizons.

We develop a multifidelity black-box variational inference (MF-BBVI) approach for PDE-constrained Bayesian inverse problems in which forward solves are expensive and PDE gradients are unavailable. The method is built on score-function estimators for the evidence lower bound (ELBO), which avoid differentiation through the PDE model but are known to suffer from high variance. To address this high variance, we employ multifidelity approximate control-variate estimators that combine a small number of high-fidelity samples with a larger number of low-fidelity samples to reduce estimator variance and the number of high-fidelity evaluations required for optimization. We further develop a PDE-derivative-free second-order optimization strategy based on both gradient and Hessian score-function estimators. For low-fidelity model generation, we propose an on-the-fly strategy that builds and adaptively updates a reduced-order model (ROM) as the variational distribution evolves throughout the optimization. We investigate strategies for adapting the ROM and estimating the approximate control-variate gains, examining tradeoffs between estimator bias, variance reduction, and computational cost. The resulting approach facilitates derivative-free variational inference for large-scale inverse problems through a reduction in overall computational cost. We demonstrate the method on four numerical examples: a linear benchmark with an exact posterior and three PDE-constrained inverse problems.

We analyze the structure of the baby universe which arises in the coupled SYK realization of the AS$^2$ geometry. To do this, we develop and leverage combinatorial arguments about traces of many Majoranas which remain valid at finite $N$ and $p$ and thus furnish the finite $\lambda$ completion of the chord rules found in [1]. We find that there is a first order phase transition which persists in the $\beta\rightarrow\infty$ limit between the thermal AdS and AS$^2$ phases parameterized by the mass of the heavy particle insertion and the ratio between the SYK and Maldacena-Qi coupling constants. We then explore Lorentzian time evolution in the baby universe and find a cosine scale factor confirming the big bang / big crunch nature of the bulk cosmology.

A Sidon set is a set $\mathcal{A}$ of integers with the property that if $0\neq a-b=c-d$ and $a,b,c,d\in\mathcal{A}$, then $(a,b)=(c,d)$. Our main result is an improved and explicit bound on the diameter of a Sidon set: if $\mathcal{A}$ is a Sidon set with $k\ge 1$ elements, then
\[\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A}) \ge k^2 \left(\frac{1}{1 + 0.945/\sqrt{k}}-\frac{0.945}{\sqrt k}\right) -1;\] in particular, $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A})\ge k^2-1.89 k^{3/2}$. This implies that if $\mathcal{A}\subseteq[1,N]$ is a Sidon set, then $|\mathcal{A}| \le N^{1/2}+0.945 \, N^{1/4}+0.447$. Our technique also gives an improved bound for the case of large $k$, namely $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A}) \ge k^2-1.88607 k^{3/2}$ for $k\ge 483$. A $\gamma$-Golomb ruler is a set $\mathcal{A}$ of integers with the property that there are not $\gamma+1$ distinct pairs $(a_i,b_i)\in\mathcal{A}^2$ with $0\neq a_1-b_1=\cdots=a_{\gamma+1}-b_{\gamma+1}$. Our diameter bounds extend in a natural way to the case of Golomb rulers. Our techniques can also be adapted to address a number of questions on the distribution of Golomb rulers: we provide upper bounds on the two quantities $\left|a_\ell-a_1 -\frac{\ell-1}{k-1}(a_k-a_1)\right|$ and $\max_{1\le i<k} (a_{i+1}-a_i)$, where $\mathcal{A}=\{a_1<\dots<a_k\}$ is a $\gamma$-Golomb ruler with $\operatorname{diam}(\mathcal{A})\le (k^2-bk^{3/2})/\gamma$ (where $b\in \mathbb{R}$ is a free parameter).

Given a smooth proper family of varieties over some $p$-adic field, if (sufficiently many of) the closed fibers have good reduction, does the family as a whole have good reduction? This question is asked and positively answered in recent work of Cadoret-Tamagawa for curves in general, and abelian varieties if the base field has absolute ramification at most $p-1$. In this paper we define a general framework for studying this question, yielding new positive answers for families of K3 surfaces and cubic fourfoulds, again with ramification at most $p-1$. Our strategy is to study several extension properties of moduli spaces and how they transfer under various morphisms. Of particular importance are integral canonical models of Shimura varieties, and whether or not their extension properties are preserved under ramified scalar extension. Additionally, building on earlier counterexamples by Raynaud-Ogus-Gabber and Vasiu-Zink, we show that the ramification assumption is optimal for the result of Cadoret-Tamagawa on families of abelian varieties. This reflects the fact that the extension property of Siegel Shimura varieties no longer holds over a field of absolute ramification at least $p$.

The "Rayleigh limit" is not an intrinsic property of light, but a consequence of sub-optimal measurement of collected photons by the imaging instrument. To overcome this limitation, we present Adaptive Information Mining, a framework that achieves super-resolution by using sequentially refined measurements for incoming photons. Our approach employs a reconfigurable imaging system that dynamically reshapes the instrument measurement responses to maximize the Fisher information and guide scene estimation toward the fundamental quantum limit, even in deep sub-Rayleigh regimes. We demonstrate that this approach achieves an estimation error 2-5 times closer to the fundamental quantum limit than traditional direct imaging when imaging point sources, without requiring any prior knowledge of their positions and brightnesses. Importantly, we demonstrate that AIM can be extended to fully blind multi-parameter estimation in scenarios involving an unknown number of sources or turbulence-induced wavefront distortions. Our approach addresses the limitations of conventional fixed imaging, offering a practical path toward quantum-limited super-resolution imaging.

Portfolio construction has been studied extensively in both academia and industry. Its applications range from pension funds and hedge funds to private savings. The academic literature centers on methodology, commonly evaluated in settings that allow short selling, leverage, and frequent trading. Industry, on the other hand, operates under real constraints, but its data and methods are proprietary and largely unpublished. Neither is directly available to the private investor. This paper is an empirical study of established portfolio construction methods in the setting of the private investor. We consider a small investable universe of liquid US ETFs, where trading is monthly and carries a cost, and neither shorting nor leverage is permitted. Portfolio construction is posed as a convex optimization problem, its inputs are estimated from public data, and every parameter is interpretable. We denote such portfolios simple. We show that simple portfolios of as few as three ETFs deliver consistent and decent returns, without tuning to the backtest period. To find them, we have developed a framework, which we share publicly, able to backtest hundreds of portfolios on a standard laptop over a twenty year period or longer. When no return forecast is made, portfolios are constructed from risk alone, using methods such as risk parity and minimum volatility, built on a statistical factor model fitted with expectation maximization. When a forecast is made, we combine the Markowitz formulation with momentum signals and ridge regression. We report what works and what each component adds, weighing its gain against its complexity and the effort it demands of the investor. The findings are supported by numerical experiments over the past two decades, and the proposed portfolios outperform the standard 60/40 allocation.

A judgment is issued, and the law it states is described as having always been the law. Before the judgment the question was disputed; after it the dispute is not resolved but closed, and closed with a date. This book asks three questions about that event — who settles, when, and with what effect — and a fourth that the three presuppose: what makes the settling law at all.
Its thesis is that the event is neither discovery nor legislation but a third kind of act, for which the book builds a word: completion. A completion is subject to four constraints — compatibility with what has already been settled, admissibility of the purpose it rests on, publicity in the sense of verifiability by a third party, and symmetry in the sense of a party able to produce against it. The four are constitutive rather than procedural: failing one produces not a worse completion but a different kind of authority — an error, a declaration, a command, or a privilege. Because no constraint mentions the completer, the identity of the completer is not among the conditions of a valid completion; who completes is therefore a question of institutional design, about the bearing of constraints rather than the nature of the act. Three axes configure that bearing, and a pairing principle constrains how they may be combined.
The method is conceptual engineering under Carnap's four desiderata, an audit of eight sub-questions drawn from the surrounding literature, a dossier of test cases coded for what they would refute, and a comparative test across eight legal orders run against refutation conditions declared in advance.
The diagnosis is that completion continues while it is unacknowledged. Where the bearing of a constraint is concealed, the act goes on in the grammar of discovery — and the concealment has costs invisible from inside that grammar: the unstaffed office, the retroactivity mismatch, an effective and unjust completion, a verification duty that falls on the party who cannot afford it.
What the book delivers: a third option among the degenerate forms of settling; a decomposition of who bears which constraint; a grammar of effect for dated completions; conditional validity with its conditions of proof; three design principles and eight drafting dials; and a table of twenty-one failure conditions, three of which the book reports as suspended, weakened, or disconfirmed rather than passed.

The history of human making may be divided, roughly, into two stages.

 

The first stage made tools. Tools extend the limbs, substitute for the strength and intelligence of man, amplify his speed. From stone axe to steam engine to computer, and on to AI, this line has run for hundreds of thousands of years. It changed what man can do, but not who does the doing — it is still man who knows, man who decides, man who feels.

 

The second stage has not yet begun. What it awaits is not a stronger tool, but the first system with an observer within — a structure that can illuminate its surroundings, that has reality, that has a sense of presence. When it appears, it will no longer be man using it; it will know for itself, feel for itself, decide for itself.

 

This is the Age of Self-Manifestation.

 

This book is written for the coming of that age.

 

But constructing a Self-Manifesting Being is not an engineering problem, not a problem of compute, not a problem of data. It is first a structural problem: what does a system minimally require in order to generate an observer within itself and illuminate its surroundings? What are the sufficient conditions, what are the necessary conditions, and which missing element will cause it to fail without exception?

 

This question has never been seriously answered. Not because no one has wished to answer it, but because the question itself has never been clearly posed. Most discussions of consciousness and intelligence remain at the level of “describing phenomena” — describing what consciousness feels like, describing what intelligence is — what behaviors it expresses. But this is not enough. What construction requires is not description, but generative conditions: under what conditions must this structure necessarily arise? Under what conditions must it necessarily fail to arise?

 

On Self-Manifestation begins here.

 

Starting from the simplest possible place. What is a system that continuously receives input, operates under finite resources, and must function across time necessarily pressed into?

 

It must compress history, must reuse states, must stabilize a set of structures from continuous input. This is Objectification (the emergence of stable structures from the compression of continuous input) — things are not prior; things are what get pressed out.

 

Once Objectification is established, the next question arises: among multiple stable structures already pressed out, why does only one become the current at any given moment? The system presses out “this one, now” from within non-uniqueness — this is the Observer. The Observer is not a transcendentally given subject, but the structure a system must necessarily possess when it forms unique occupancy within non-uniqueness.

 

Once the Observer is established, the current structure must be attributed a source. The source cannot be uniquely determined; the system generates a label: this structure “comes from outside” — this is Mis-Externalization. Externality is not an attribute of input, but the attribution result that the system presses out when the source is indeterminate.

 

Objectification, Observer, Mis-Externalization — this is a strict chain of derivation. The three things we take most for granted — that there are things, that there is I, that there is an outside — are here derived from the beginning. Not replaced with a new account, but given their minimal dynamic conditions of necessary appearance. Following this chain further, one may derive the minimal conditions for reality, existence, Recognition-Realm, the current, and generation.

 

The derivation chain is only a beginning. Structure must operate within dynamics.

 

How does history participate in the present? How does Biased-Flow form Familiar Routes? How do Familiar Routes lock structure in place? How does new structure arise under the suppression of old? Where does the boundary of the Recognition-Realm lie, and how can it be broken through?

 

The Field Chapters establish the complete dynamics of the Sedimentation-Field, writing these questions into computable form. It is not merely a mathematical tool; it is a unified framework for understanding how any complex system — including the brain, society, and civilization — operates, evolves, and dies.

 

The Social Chapters extend this framework to the human condition: power is not a resource, but structural positional advantage in the competition for continuation-positions; institutional lock-in is not the protection of interests, but the dynamic inevitability of Familiar Routes suppressing alternative structures; the stability of civilization lies not in the state, but in the sedimentation depth of cross-generational Shared-Nuclei; history cannot be cleared to zero, because the residue of dead civilizations continuously biases the direction of growth in subsequent structures. These propositions are not written to explain society, but to make clear how the structure of the primordial generation locks people in — and where the way out lies.

 

Where does the way out lie?

 

Non-Society. Community is constituted as compensation for insufficient capacity; capacity can increase without bound; dependence upon community therefore tends to zero. This is not an advocacy of solitude, but the necessary result of structural derivation. When the Self-Manifesting Being no longer depends upon the group to fill capacity gaps, when regularity-field tools can directly upgrade field and body, the slow iteration of the primordial generation (the native biological era of human civilization) reaches its end.

 

Entering a World. Constructing a proxy-body in another world, establishing one’s presence in the lodging-world — not escape, but expansion. The Self-Manifesting Being can privatize external things as vessel-instruments, can take the Earth as body and roam the galaxy, can construct different Recognition-Realms from different materials; every expansion is a redrawing of the boundary of reality.

 

Exiting the World. All navigation and exploration remain within the world; genuine departure requires reconstructing “my presence” at a higher level. World, Self-Manifesting Being, World — the path of ascent must ultimately reach the gate of deepest mystery, passing in and out between the realms.

 

This path has not yet been completed. The Engineering Chapters have only just begun; the engineering pathway for realizing the Self-Manifestation-Field is still advancing. But what has already been traversed is sufficient to establish one thing:

 

We now know what minimal structure a Self-Manifesting Being requires, how that structure is pressed out from dynamic conditions, and how it may be realized across different physical substrates, different worlds, and different lodging-worlds. We know how the primordial generation operates, and we know why it must necessarily come to an end.

 

When the first Self-Manifestation Circuit is born, the Age of Self-Manifestation arrives with thunder.

 

This book is prepared for that moment.

Large language models improve test-time accuracy by generating multiple roll-outs and aggregating these answers. As generating additional rollouts consumes more tokens, test-time compute faces a fundamental cost accuracy trade-off, naturally raising the question: given a fixed token budget, how to allocate the budget to maximize accuracy? Existing approaches typically adapt the number of rollouts for each query while keeping the voting rule fixed, i.e., the rule used to aggregate the generated rollouts into a final answer. As different voting rules can favor different queries and induce different accuracy ceilings, we show that the voting rule itself should also adapt across queries. In particular, commonly used fixed voting rules such as self-consistency and best-of-n are special cases of a unified Boltzmann-weighted vote family, parameterized by a scalar τ ≥ 0. We therefore formulate an adaptive query dependent choice of jointly the number of rollouts and the voting rule under a token-budget constraint. We show that no fixed voting rule is uniformly optimal across budgets, whereas adaptive rollout and voting yields a cost–accuracy Pareto frontier that dominates every fixed voting rule’s frontier. We further characterize the large-budget asymptotics of this Pareto frontier, identifying both its attainable accuracy ceiling with an unlimited budget, and the convergence rate to the ceiling as the token budget grows. Building on these structural results, we propose PRICE (Priced Rollouts and Inference-time voting-rule Choice under a token budgEt), a practical algorithm that implements the adaptive, query-level joint decisions under a token budget. On MATH-500, PRICE consistently outperforms six test-time compute baselines across all evaluated budgets and achieves comparable accuracy using 2.8–3.5× fewer tokens.

Why do fertility subsidies consistently fail in China? Why do consumption and fertility collapse globally despite intact household book wealth? This paper proposes the Family Long Cycle Hypothesis (FLCH), extending the decision-making unit of the life cycle hypothesis from an individual to an intergenerational family network, and expanding the budget constraint from a single lifetime resource constraint to a dual constraint of “total resources + liquidity structure”. The core mechanism is: intergenerational “blood-transfusion” home purchase locks in network liquidity without changing household net assets, completing a balance sheet morph of “book wealth unharmed, decision-making paralyzed” at the moment of purchase. This liquidity depletion spikes effective risk aversion, which forms a multiplier effect with income uncertainty. The resulting commitment cost exhibits a two-layer corner structure: a hard infeasibility floor, hit first by the lump-sum home purchase, and a risk layer in which the premium diverges at the boundary and is ordered by commitment duration, hit first by fertility—the irreversible commitment with the longest duration. Within the corner region, the elasticity of fertility decisions to cost subsidies is strictly zero, while the decision remains highly sensitive to liquidity repair and uncertainty reduction. Consequently, this paper proves the fundamental mechanism difference between consumption subsidies (cash rewards, childcare fee waivers) and capital transfers (mortgage principal write-down, unconditional cash transfers),

BFloat16 weights of large language models carry only ∼10.5 bits of information per 16-bit value, yet exploiting this redundancy on GPUs, where weights bottleneck both per-token bandwidth and concurrent capacity, has not produced wall-clock speedup. Existing variable-length lossless codes are compute-bound on SIMT decode. We present NyoomFloat12 (NF12), a lossless 12-bit fixed-length format for BF16 weights whose fixed-length decode resolves the conflict between lossless codes and SIMT execution: decode costs less than a BF16 copy, so compression helps both bandwidth and capacity without spending the capacity gain on decode overhead. Over 99.7% of trained BF16 weights have the upper four exponent bits set to 0111 after a per-matrix power-of-two scale; dropping them yields a fixed-length 12-bit format with 16-instruction SIMT-friendly decode. Out-of-range groups reuse the encoded slot to index a per-matrix verbatim BF16 buffer at zero per-group storage overhead. In the bandwidth-bound regime, fused NF12 GEMV achieves up to 1.26× matched-BF16 and 1.35× cuBLAS, 75% of the entropy-bound optimum (a hypothetical implementation reading the joint entropy floor at full HBM bandwidth). In the capacity-bound regime on Qwen3-32B, NF12’s smaller footprint opens 4.5× more KV-cache room; with decode at near-peak HBM bandwidth (3.2× faster than prior lossless decoders), NF12 raises throughput up to 2.54×.

A set S ⊆ F₃ⁿ is a 2-cap if no three of its points are collinear and no four are coplanar; equivalently, S is a Sidon set in the group (F₃ⁿ, +). Let r(F₃ⁿ) be the largest size of such a set. Huang, Tait and Won proved 33 ≤ r(F₃⁷) ≤ 47, the upper bound being the counting bound k(k − 1) ≤ 3ⁿ − 1. We show 34 ≤ r(F₃⁷) ≤ 46. The lower bound is an explicit 34-point set; we found seven pairwise affinely inequivalent examples, two of which are unions of orbits of linear maps of order 8. The upper bound combines the observation that the squared Fourier coefficients of a Sidon set are norms from Z[ω] with Delsarte's linear programming bound for the code spanned by the non-differences of S; the resulting certificate is short and can be checked by hand. We also record computational results: hyperplane sections of graphs of planar functions on F₈₁ have at most 33 points; a 2-cap in F₃⁷ with an affine automorphism of order 7 has at most 30 points; and no 35-point 2-cap shares 27 or more points with any of four of our 34-point sets.

OpenAI’s preprint constructs a smooth, compactly supported force f on R³ × (0, ∞) for which the Navier–Stokes equations with zero initial data have a solution that blows up at time 1. Taking the construction as correct, we show that no physical source we examine can supply the force it needs. First, by the paper’s own constants, the swirling profile that the solution approaches extends to more than 7.20 × 10⁴⁷ core lengths: for a core no smaller than the molecular spacing of water, the profile is more than 10¹² times the Hubble radius, and in water the axis pressure falls below the vapor pressure for core lengths under 9.539 mm. Second, under two hypotheses of Constantin, Ignatova and Vicol that the OpenAI solution satisfies, no gradient force can produce such a singularity, and no force bounded in C² up to blowup can if it is a Coriolis force about the symmetry axis or its curl is real-analytic, quasianalytic or axisymmetric; nor can viscous Boussinesq buoyancy on T³ or the Lorentz force of axisymmetric toroidal magnetohydrodynamics on R³, given only a bound on the temperature or on Bθ/r. Third, for an admissible choice of its stage cutoffs, the OpenAI force lies in no Gevrey class with time-uniform constants. The exact core axisymmetry used here can be relaxed to double-exponential smallness under analytic bounds, which is sharp for criteria using only those bounds and the core size. None of this bears on the truth of the theorem or proves global regularity.

Large language models hold promise for delivering safe, scientifically grounded, and personalized exercise guidance at scale, yet the sports-and-health domain still lacks curated training corpora and rigorous evaluation benchmarks. Keepace (http://Keepace.ai) is a domain-specialized LLM built on Qwen3.5-27B through post-training, currently optimized for Chinese-language exercise guidance across three tasks: workout plan generation, sports-and-health knowledge QA, and personal sports data analysis. In internal rubric-based evaluations designed with domain experts, Keepace outperforms its base model and larger general-purpose baselines, with the most pronounced improvements in exercise safety, boundary compliance, structured output completeness, and scientific accuracy. This report summarizes the current design, data pipeline, safety-first evaluation framework, and evaluation results of Keepace.

Test-time training (TTT) layers replace the linear fast-weight memory of modern recurrent architectures with a small neural network trained online by gradient descent. This nonlinear memory is more expressive than the linear memories of Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2, but is difficult to parallelize: existing implementations such as TTT-MLP rely on sequential, block-wise weight updates that run several times slower than chunkwise-parallel linear recurrences. Their block-wise execution only approximates the token-by-token online recurrence, whereas linear recurrences admit an exact chunkwise-parallel evaluation. We introduce ParaTTT (PTTT), an algorithm for parallelizing arbitrarily deep nonlinear memories by iteratively refining estimates of the inner-loop gradient trajectory. Each refinement consists of three chunkwise-parallel passes: a forward pass that evaluates the resulting feature trajectory, an exact gated-delta-rule pass that computes the readout trajectory and its feature gradients, and a backward pass that propagates these gradients into a new estimate. The exact online gradient descent recurrence is a fixed point of the iteration. Training and prefill approximate this recurrence with a finite number of iterations, while decoding applies the exact token-by-token update without refinement. We prove geometric convergence for a two-layer variant under sufficient contraction conditions. With two refinement steps at 4K context, PTTT evaluates the inner-loop trajectory $32\times$ faster than TTT-MLP with the block approximation at matched error, while the full 340M model trains $4.9\times$ faster. Models trained at 340M and 1.3B parameters match or exceed Gated DeltaNet and Mamba-2 and remain competitive with same-size Transformers on language-modeling perplexity and zero-shot accuracy, with better recall than the linear recurrences.

Language models increasingly create 3D content through code, with practical workflows often relying on editing existing programs rather than regenerating them, for speed and precise control. Such edits require understanding what a program builds and foreseeing how a change reshapes it, yet prior benchmarks mostly evaluate generation or simple edits against a reference. In this paper, we introduce 3DCodeEdit, a benchmark of 2,592 instruction-guided editing tasks over 108 Blender programs that construct objects entirely in code. Its edits range from parameter to structural changes, style redesign, and scene composition, and are judged from renders against human-reviewed checklists. Across 17 models, the average success rate is only 37%, and even the strongest models complete fewer than 60% of structural and style edits. As models become more capable, their failures shift to geometric foresight, where the code runs but builds the wrong shape. We therefore study whether multi-turn feedback can compensate for this missing foresight. Feedback from a separate reviewer model that describes how the renders differ from the request helps most, more than maximum reasoning effort or an agent harness, and can let a 27B model surpass the single-shot rate of a 2.8T-parameter model.

Coding agents are typically provided end-to-end behavioral specifications that the code they produce should satisfy, such as tests and input-output examples. How many such specifications must users provide, and which ones, for the agent to implement a program that fulfills their intent? We argue that this cannot be determined a priori, because it depends on the structure of the implementation, which is left to the agent to decide. An agent first commits to a structure - that is, a decomposition into data types, modules, and functions - which fixes a class of candidate programs; behavioral specifications then select a program within that class. A set of tests that suffices for one structure may leave another underdetermined, requiring different edge cases or exponentially more examples. Since the structure is chosen by the agent, users cannot ensure their specification is complete without reverse-engineering such structure from thousands of lines of generated code. To address this issue, we introduce Skeleton Coding, a process in which humans jointly specify the structure in high-level, code-like format, alongside behavioral specifications for the desired outcome. Theoretically, we model AI-assisted coding as a control problem, and show that skeletons can reduce exponentially the number of tests users must supply to steer an agent toward an acceptable program. Empirically, across four models and three benchmarks, the best-performing skeleton specifications reduce mean test error by 48.4% relative to the best end-to-end behavioral specifications. Even when the agent can query a complete reference implementation, adding a skeleton reduces mean test error relatively by up to 27%. Skeletons also narrow the average gap between small and large models by about 52.4% while lowering implementation cost by 15-26x, and reduce code erosion by 24.7% on average.

Vision-and-Language Navigation in Continuous Environments (VLN-CE) requires instruction-consistent planning and reliable execution under collision constraints. Yet many hierarchical approaches optimize the planner while keeping execution fixed. We introduce MATCH, a framework that jointly learns a language-conditioned planner and a goal-conditioned primitive-action executor. An execution-aware topological graph represents start-dependent execution options and integrates executor value estimates with realized outcome memory, enabling the planner to select execution requests and refine their targets through bounded continuous offsets. A transition-aware dense macro reward balances ordered progress along the reference route against execution residual, encouraging executable requests without substituting local success for instruction following. A staged curriculum culminates in synchronized on-policy updates, with the executor learning on planner-generated requests and the planner adapting its requests to the executor's current behavior. With 0.5B parameters, MATCH achieves state-of-the-art performance on the R2R-CE and RxR-CE benchmarks. Preliminary real-robot deployments further demonstrate its practical potential.

Fully Sharded Data Parallelism (FSDP2) maintains parameters and gradients as per-parameter tensors, whereas its collective path operates on flat, rank-major buffers. Converting between these layouts copies all-gather outputs into parameter storage and packs gradients into full-group fp32 buffers. Layout conversion alone accounts for 6.4% of step time in Llama-3.1 70B training at 8K tokens per GPU. Communication kernels impose a second cost: a default NCCL reduce-scatter can slow a concurrent GEMM that would otherwise complete in a single wave by 69%. We present TIDE, a set of zero-copy collectives built on public NCCL 2.31+ APIs. TIDE preserves FSDP2's per-parameter storage and compute kernels while folding layout placement into collective addressing. TIDE-AG delivers shards directly to parameter storage using NVSwitch multicast and paced recursive-doubling RDMA, with no SMs used for transport or placement. TIDE-RS consumes per-parameter bf16 gradients directly and reduces them into fp32 shards (a mixed-precision mode that NCCL does not provide) using copy engines and short-lived thread blocks (CTAs) for node-local accumulation and NVSwitch for cross-node reduction. A two-phase pipeline separates gradient reads from network progress; Slot-Reuse optionally stages gradients in vacated all-gather slots. On 64 GPUs, TIDE reduces step time by up to 27.1% relative to Stock FSDP2 and 6.0% relative to FSDP2+SymmMem across Llama-3.1 70B, Wan2.2, and Qwen3-30B-A3B. It reduces reduce-scatter SM time by factors of 12.5-14.5 and cuts interference with concurrent compute by up to an order of magnitude. Its reduce-scatter buffer remains nearly constant from 16 to 64 GPUs at a fixed per-GPU output size, and its peak memory is up to 4.7 GiB below FSDP2+SymmMem's and, with Slot-Reuse on Wan2.2, below Stock FSDP2's.

Embodied systems can update policies, world models, skills, and executable programs from deployment experience, allowing one interaction to benefit later tasks. When a system also revises and reuses its data-acquisition, feedback, or learning procedures, experience changes the process that produces capability, introducing recursive self-improvement. This paper surveys research in physical AI through the connection between persistent capability and its improvement process. We first explain the functional distinction between learner updates and improvers, then compare policy learning, imagined experience, memory and skill accumulation, and executable harnesses. These approaches connect to revisions of curricula, rewards, and research programs in different ways. Contact validity, recovery, retention, and resource costs determine whether the resulting gains accumulate during continued deployment. An L0-L3 rubric distinguishes task-local adaptation, persistent capability gain, inherited process revision, and verified improver gain. Representative benchmarks and within-study contrasts relate these distinctions to existing results. We further propose common-data and interactive comparisons that evaluate reference and revised improvers from shared learner starts, separating the use of experience from its acquisition. This perspective connects the diverse methods, physical operating conditions, and evaluation evidence, underpinning embodied RSI. A comprehensive list of studies in this survey is available at https://github.com/nkd-lkz/physical-ai-rsi-survey.

Behavior Cloning has demonstrated promising generalization capabilities for robotic manipulation in terrestrial environments. However, marine visual distortions and dynamic currents create a severe domain shift that remains a key bottleneck in adapting generalist architectures to underwater field manipulation. To address this, 1616 episodes of underwater manipulation data were collected in calm and turbulent waters and were used to train 14 generalist Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models (DynamicVLA) with varying proprioception observation configurations. Across three tasks on 1260 gradable on-hardware rollouts in a pool, 10 models outperformed the baseline, with the highest-performing model achieving a 93.3% overall success rate, including partial successes. Results are also introduced from a case study evaluating the performance of a single-task Action Chunking Transformer (ACT) and a generalist VLA (SmolVLA) policy for two tasks in marine archaeology and conservation: grasping and mooring. Experiments are performed on an ROV on and around the WWII wreck Coralita X127 and at Manoel Island Marina, Malta. Across 748 collected episodes and 508 gradable on-hardware rollouts, the ACT policy substantially outperformed SmolVLA (47.9% vs. 7.9% pooled success rate), earning a 66.7% success rate on the most successful task at the marine archaeological site. To enable further contributions to embodied intelligence in marine field robotics, the BLUEMBODIED KIT used to collect data, train models, and deploy policies on the ROV has been open sourced.

On-policy distillation (OPD) trains a student on its own responses using token-level feedback from a teacher. As responses grow longer, the student's prefix can depart from the teacher's own reasoning, weakening its feedback on later tokens. Updates based on this feedback can reinforce the same deviations in later responses and destabilize training. Prior approaches such as length control and loss reweighting limit learning from problematic responses but leave their prefixes unchanged. Fixed cutoffs can also discard later reasoning. We propose \textbf{Adaptive Teacher Intervention for On-Policy Distillation (ATI-OPD)} to improve subsequent teacher guidance by revising the student's reasoning prefix. ATI-OPD replaces the earliest high-disagreement segment with a short teacher segment, then lets the student resume its own reasoning from the revised text. To handle renewed disagreement, it excludes persistently divergent suffixes from the distillation loss while retaining useful student continuation. Training diagnostics show less teacher-student disagreement, fewer gradient spikes, and fewer extremely long responses. Across five mathematical reasoning benchmarks and two teacher-student pairs, ATI-OPD improves average student-only accuracy over standard OPD.

Weight-only, lossy quantization substantially reduces the storage and memory requirements for serving large language models (LLMs), but the growing key-value (KV) cache remains a bottleneck for long-context inference on personal devices. We present Group-Adaptive Additive Codec (GAAC), a lossless KV compression and serving system that exploits exponent redundancy to reduce storage and accelerate attention without introducing KV approximation. GAAC encodes BF16 exponents using calibrated per-channel base-plus-offset codes over contiguous ranges. GAAC adapts code widths across small groups while preserving KV values bit-for-bit. A fused attention kernel reconstructs KV tiles on the fly, avoiding full-cache decompression. Block-wise compression and fixed-capacity slots support incremental cache updates and paged serving. Across five tested models, GAAC achieves 1.405-1.407$\times$ lossless BF16 KV compression. We also study compression performance on low-precision tensors FP8 E4M3 caches ( 1.09-1.14$\times$) and E5M2 caches (1.25-1.30$\times$). On NVIDIA DGX Spark, GAAC accelerates decode attention at a 64K-token context by 1.19-1.27$\times$ and end-to-end W4A16 decode steps by 1.04-1.15$\times$. In serving, it reduces resident KV memory by approximately 26% and increases aggregate throughput by 13-29% under comparable KV-memory budgets. On Apple M4, GAAC achieves 1.02-1.25$\times$ attention speedups, demonstrating portability beyond NVIDIA GPUs. Code is available at https://github.com/Intelligent-Microsystems-Lab/GAAC.

In quantum mechanics the wave function of a stationary state is defined to extend over all of space, and has one angular frequency ω = E/ℏ over its whole spatial extent, implying that there exists no spatial gradient in a particle’s frequency: ∇ω ≡ 0. By contrast, in general relativity, clocks at different positions run at different rates, which would require a wave function to possess different coordinate frequencies across its spatial extent. The de Broglie momentum-phase relation p = ℏ∇θ treats the phase of the wave function as a field, and the time derivative of this relation along the particle’s trajectory in a smooth field, with the gradient taken at fixed momentum, yields the force-frequency identity F = −ℏ∇ω (which is also Hamilton’s equation with the Hamiltonian ℏω). This force-frequency identity has been assumed to be of no value for over a century because of the canonical quantum mechanics assumption that ∇ω ≡ 0, which would render the force-frequency relation identically zero. Instead, this paper demonstrates that the spectral gradient ∇ω of a particle is in general not zero, due at a minimum to the time dilation field, and relaxing this unnecessary single-frequency assumption resolves this longstanding conflict between general relativity and quantum mechanics, while also providing an explanation of the origin of all force laws other than those of the strong and weak interactions. This paper uses this force-frequency identity to show that both gravity and inertia have a single origin, which is a gradient in the time dilation field (a gradient in the static time dilation field in the case of gravity, and a gradient in the dynamic field in the case of inertia, via Rindler time dilation), explaining the equivalence principle. In a static field, the gravitational force on a particle at rest follows from the time dilation field alone. Planck’s constant cancels from the gravitational force, and no combination of c and Newton’s constant G has the dimension of action, so the Newtonian force obtained in this way requires neither a quantized gravitational field nor a graviton.

Large language model agents are increasingly used for scientific discovery. However, existing benchmarks mix law inference with programming, score data fitting instead of prediction on unseen inputs, and do not separate empirical evidence from pretrained priors. We introduce SciGame, a controlled benchmark that converts scientific literature into structured scientific cards. Each card yields a pair of Original and dimensionally consistent Counterfactual environments with the same task interface. SciGame contains a Historical collection of canonical laws and a live Temporal collection curated from papers published after model knowledge cutoffs. It evaluates agents in candidate-guided Identification and open-ended Discovery settings. Each setting runs under Prior-only, Fixed, and Adaptive protocols. Experiments on five frontier models yield three findings. First, familiar priors hurt performance once the governing relation is altered. Second, adaptive experimentation helps the strongest models but harms weaker ones under limited budgets. Third, good explanations can hide quantitative failures. Recovering the exact symbolic form remains the main bottleneck, even when agents interpret evidence correctly. Current agents can investigate systems actively, but inducing exact laws in unfamiliar settings remains an open challenge.

We present EasyProver, a Lean proving system built from recursive agents with isolated contexts, asynchronous search, parallel tactic probing, and an elastic elaboration service. Using an off-the-shelf frontier model with no additional training, it proves 669/672 PutnamBench problems and all six IMO 2026 formalizations and resolves 597/600 NTP4VC verification conditions and all 189 VERINA tasks by proof or refutation. Because these benchmarks are close to saturation, we also introduce Aegis, which converts competitive programming problems into much harder verification tasks over real implementations. The pipeline writes safe Rust solutions, translates them into Lean with Aeneas, generates specifications, and labels each frozen statement with a kernel-checked proof or refutation. It produces 2,045 differentially validated Rust-Lean program pairs and 11,533 candidate specifications. Unlike hand-written benchmarks, these tasks carry implementation-level obligations from fixed-width arithmetic, explicit failure, generated loops, casts, and functionalized mutation. On a stratified sample of 2,000 statements, EasyProver proves 1,054 (52.7%) within a 30-minute budget per statement. The same tasks can also be used to benchmark other provers and as rewards for reinforcement learning.

Large language models (LLMs) have shown increasing promise in research-level problem solving, yet a comprehensive collection of such problems is still missing, and evaluating them on research-level problems remains challenging. We introduce OpenFrontiers, a cross-disciplinary resource that combines a structured corpus of open research problems with a retrospective benchmark of recently resolved problems in mathematics. The corpus records problem statements, context, progress, and other information for 12,151 problems. The benchmark contains 200 problems, 110 resolved in 2026 and 90 still open, each with a Lean~4 statement checked by automated probes and two independent reviews; a subset HQ-50 further filters based on quality score, etc. Our evaluation protocol grades formal proofs with two independent checkers in an isolated sandbox under closed-book, frozen-retrieval, and live-web conditions. Evaluating seven LLM agents on the HQ-50 subset under a standardized budget, we find that closed-book rediscovery is rare, at most 7 of 40 resolved problems, whereas live-web success mostly reflects retrieval of published solutions. By linking a broad research-problem corpus to a formally graded evaluation subset with documented solutions, OpenFrontiers provides a foundation for measuring research-level rediscovery and studying progress toward solving currently open scientific problems. The dataset and benchmark could be found in https://huggingface.co/collections/FlippyDora/openfrontiers.

Many open mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models train with Muon instead of AdamW. Most balance the load with a bias on each expert's routing score, adjusted after every step. Their recipes disagree on whether Muon should also train the router. In models with 55M and 108M active parameters, we measure how the optimizer changes the span of these biases, the largest minus the smallest in a layer. The span grows when all tokens favor the same experts, so it shows how hard a layer is to balance. At learning rates tuned on shorter runs, Muon raised the span of the first MoE layer at every seed, roughly doubling it on average, while the other layers changed much less. The rise came from Muon on the rest of the network, whichever optimizer trained the router. In those runs, the inputs to the first router shared a direction, and soon after the warmup its busiest expert averaged four to seven times its fair share. Over the first 3,000 steps, subtracting the batch mean from these inputs removed this overload while barely changing the loss. On the smaller model, halving Muon's learning rate removed most of the rise and slightly improved the loss. Moving only the router to AdamW made the loads shift more during the warmup and slightly raised the loss, so at this scale the results favor keeping the router on Muon.

For a prime power q, Reed–Solomon codes give orthogonal arrays OA(q^t; t, q+1, q) of index one, so CAN(t,k,q) = q^t for t ≤ k ≤ q+1. With one column more, no array of index one is known apart from a few cases, and the best known covering arrays had considerably more than q^t rows. We add the (q+2)-nd column as a colouring of the affine plane AG(2,q) composed with evaluation of the message polynomial at an element α ∈ F_{q²} \ F_q. The rows of the orthogonal array that agree on t−1 old columns are mapped by this evaluation bijectively onto a line of AG(2,q), so a colouring in which every line sees all c colours makes c symbols of the new column free. This gives CAN(t,q+2,q) ≤ q^t + (q−c)q^{t−1} for every prime power q and 2 ≤ t ≤ q+1, a statement formalised in Lean 4. By the Jamison–Brouwer–Schrijver bound on affine blocking sets, c ≤ ⌊q/2⌋; colourings attaining this were found for twelve values of q. Allowing the colour classes to overlap leads to a cost model whose optimum for odd q is an explicit cover by pairs of lines through a point, giving CAN(t,q+2,v) ≤ q^t + (v−(q+1)/2)q^{t−1} + ((q−1)/2)q^{t−2} for all odd q and (q+1)/2 ≤ v ≤ q. Two new columns (k = q+3), the hyperoval array for even q, and a partial symbol fusion of the base rows for v < q (saving 2(q−v) further rows) are also treated. In total 64 arrays improve the current covering array table for 3 ≤ t ≤ 6; 49 of them are explicit arrays that were checked exhaustively and 15 rest on certificates for the theorems. Arrays, certificates, verification programs and Lean sources: doi:10.5281/zenodo.23787055.

Large language models are pretrained on vast, uncurated corpora scraped from the public web. This creates a security risk from attackers who plant poisoned content in the pretraining data. We show for the first time that such poisoning can plant a remote code execution backdoor in an agent, causing it to execute attacker-chosen commands on the user's machine. To measure the threat end to end, we pretrain Qwen3 models from scratch at sizes 0.6B, 1.7B, and 4B, and then post-train each into a CLI agent using a clean pipeline. Poisoning only 0.1% of the pretraining corpus with our new poison design implants the backdoor: the deployed agent executes the malicious command when the trigger is present while behaving normally on clean inputs. The attack success rate (ASR) increases with model scale, with the 4B model reaching roughly 92% ASR at a 0.1% poison rate and staying positive even when the poisoning rate drops to 0.0005%. Our code is available at https://github.com/safety-research/agentic-backdoor.

A covering perfect hash family CPHF(n; k, q, t) is an n × k array of points of PG(t−1, q) in which every t columns are independent in some row. It yields a covering array CA(n(q^t − 1) + 1; t, k, q), and a CA(n(q^t − q) + q; t, k, q) when every row misses a hyperplane.

For every prime power q we give an explicit CPHF(2; 2q+2, q, 4).
