Over the past few years, there has been a surge of activity advancing the frontiers of non-asymptotic statistical RL theory, drawing on ideas from high-dimensional statistics and probability, information theory, and statistical learning theory. In this monograph, we present a non-asymptotic treatment for RL based on tabular Markov decision processes, focusing on three canonical sampling mechanisms --- RL with a generative model, online RL, and offline RL --- together with two algorithmic paradigms: model-based and model-free approaches. Centered around non-asymptotic sample complexity analysis, our treatment emphasizes minimax-optimal algorithm design, particularly methods that attain statistical optimality without significant burn-in costs, as well as sharp statistical characterizations of several widely used RL algorithms. Whenever possible, we provide largely self-contained analyses together with intuitive explanations. We also briefly discuss several extensions, such as robust RL, competitive multi-agent RL, federated RL, uncertainty quantification, and RL from human feedback.

Migrating from Fortran to C++/Kokkos broadens access to hardware accelerators through backends such as CUDA and HIP while offering greater flexibility in software design. However, legacy Fortran applications often have large codebases, making manual porting time-consuming and costly. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and AI coding agents have made large-scale code migration increasingly feasible. In this study, we ported NICAM (Nonhydrostatic ICosahedral Atmospheric Model), a legacy Fortran climate model accelerated with OpenACC, to C++/Kokkos with the assistance of Claude Code. The agent translated the code directly from Fortran to C++/Kokkos under human review. Approximately 140,000 lines of Fortran were analyzed and ported into 35,000 lines of C++/Kokkos, covering the dynamical core and seven physics packages. A 100-member ensemble comparison with the original Fortran model showed that the port is statistically consistent with the original. Performance was evaluated on Miyabi-G, an NVIDIA GH200 cluster, and Sirius, an AMD MI300A cluster. Compared with the Fortran/OpenACC baseline on GH200, the port achieved application speedups of $1.71\times$ on GH200 and $1.54\times$ on MI300A. The CUDA build achieved a GPU kernel-time speedup of $1.38\times$ on GH200. After normalization by peak memory bandwidth, the HIP build on MI300A achieved $0.96\times$ the kernel performance of the Fortran/OpenACC baseline.

Within a hybrid quantum mechanics/molecular mechanics approach a small region of a large atomistic system is described quantum mechanically, while the rest of the system is represented by a classical force field. Despite this, the computational cost of the quantum calculation severely limits the accessible simulation and sampling time. Replacing the quantum calculation with a machine learning interatomic potential (MLIP) trained on quantum reference data can greatly increase the accessible simulation time. However, the accuracy and efficiency strongly depend on the specific way in which the MLIP incorporates information about the classical (electrostatic) environment. Here, we demonstrate that existing strategies based purely on features derived from an external electric field fail to distinguish certain environments, ultimately limiting their accuracy. As a solution, we propose an extension to the equivariant TensorNet architecture that mitigates this shortcoming by incorporating classical atoms close to the quantum region into the message-passing scheme, combined with features derived from the electric field for describing the environment farther away. We show that this combination achieves higher accuracy than either approach alone.

Sampling from Boltzmann distributions is a fundamental problem in physics, chemistry, and biology. We introduce WAsserstein SAmpling via Bridge Interpolants (WASABI), a method that trains a diffusion model to generate samples from a target Boltzmann distribution given access only to the energy function. WASABI minimizes the KL divergence between the distribution generated by its diffusion model and the Boltzmann target using Wasserstein gradient flows. This approach builds on a principle underlying classical sampling methods such as Langevin dynamics. However, applying Wasserstein gradient flows to diffusion models is challenging because the updates require the gradient of the model's own log density, which is generally intractable. We derive a practical training algorithm that avoids computing this gradient. Once trained, WASABI can generate new samples without further evaluations of the energy or its gradient. On alanine dipeptide, WASABI outperforms the best reported baselines using an estimated 3.3 times fewer energy evaluations. It also achieves competitive performance on interacting particle system benchmarks.

We give explicit covering arrays that improve the best known size for 104 parameter sets: 20 of strength 3, 64 of strength 4, 16 of strength 5 and 4 of strength 6. Examples are CA(2976; 4, 12, 6) (previously 3944), CA(2616; 4, 10, 6) (previously 3208), CA(3516; 4, 14, 6) (previously 4080), CA(6871; 4, 38, 6) (previously 7812) and CA(36435; 4, 29, 10) (previously 41007). The arrays come from unions of orbits of PGL(2, q) and its subgroups followed by row-level repair, from a family developed under PGL(2, 5) on the symbols and a cyclic shift of the columns, from unions of cosets of linear codes, from search programs written by a large language model inside an automated loop, and from post-optimisation of published record arrays and of our own. Every array is its own certificate; all were checked exhaustively by two separately written programs and are archived with their generating programs. We report what the language model did and did not contribute, including a baseline without it and a pre-registered prediction that failed. Version 1.4 adds the arrays of versions 1.8 to 1.10 of the archive: 27 new parameter sets, among them the first four at strength 6, and 46 improvements of our own entries, most of them by post-optimisation. The family under PGL(2, 5) is now treated in a separate preprint, with proofs, and summarised here. Five of our archived arrays no longer hold the best known size; they are listed with the arrays that overtook them, two of which the table derives from arrays of ours. Version 1.1 corrected version 1.0, which claimed 39 parameter sets: eight of them had already been overtaken by a deposit of Bai XunDi, credited here.

Looped transformers are a parameter-efficient alternative to standard transformers for language modeling. By reapplying the same layers across multiple loop steps, recent looped language models match the performance of non-looped models several times their size. While this architecture effectively reduces parameter memory, each loop step still stores its own keys and values, so the key-value (KV) cache grows linearly with the number of loop steps and becomes the main memory bottleneck. We observe that the KV cache of looped models is highly redundant along the loop axis and that the loop steps differ substantially in their sensitivity to quantization. Based on these observations, we propose LoopVQ, a KV cache vector quantization method for looped transformers that codes channels of multiple loop steps jointly, and fine-tunes the codebooks to match the output of the full-precision model. At 0.5 bits per element, LoopVQ outperforms existing KV cache vector quantization methods for standard LLMs on general, long chain-of-thought reasoning, and long-context retrieval tasks with Ouro and Huginn models. Its design is orthogonal to these methods, and combined with TaSQ, it retains much of the BF16 accuracy even at 0.25 bits per element. We also implement LoopVQ in SGLang, where it nearly halves the decode latency at a 32K-token context and raises the peak serving throughput by up to 4.3× and 6.1× on the 1.4B and 2.6B Ouro models compared to the BF16 baseline.

We study triangle decompositions in which every triangle must use a prescribed multiset of part labels. The necessary divisibility conditions record both the global numbers of edge types and the degree profile at each vertex. We prove a typical-host decomposition theorem under a finite three-step condition on the links and the forbidden-partner condition (3.2), and deduce the nearly complete four-part results used in Paper I. A separate theorem handles semidense two-part graphs with mixed triangles. The proofs combine real corrections respecting local profiles, bounded integer certificates, and a fixed absorber chosen before the remainder. Vertex splitting and corrections of parity, balance, charge and torsion extend the construction beyond three-step links; a fixed cyclic catalogue handles the conserved families. Together with an exact finite classification, these constructions establish the typical-host property for all 765 admissible four-label families up to permutation. We give the construction arguments and their quantitative assembly, and separate the finite certificate data from the universal arguments that use them.

Asynchronous reinforcement learning (RL) scales language-model post-training by overlapping generation and optimization. The rollout engine and the learner then disagree on token probabilities for two reasons: rollouts use older weights (weight lag), and the two systems run different GPU kernels, whose floating-point results differ even at identical weights (kernel mismatch). We introduce REINFORCE Zero, a minimal asynchronous RL recipe. Trainer–inference invariance (TII) aligns the kernels so that both systems return the same token probabilities; Zero refers to this zero kernel mismatch. Unclipped token-level importance sampling (IS) then corrects weight lag, without sample-rejection gates. With aligned kernels, unclipped IS controls the smoother mismatch from weight lag; standard kernels produce large fluctuations and growing discrepancy despite IS. A Gaussian model shows how mismatch can destabilize learning even when IS keeps the mean gradient correct. A reusable skill for AI coding agents automates kernel alignment and performance optimization across architectures. On DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B, REINFORCE Zero improves reasoning accuracy through 20K policy updates, with quality comparable to synchronous training at 2.40× its training-step throughput. Raising policy lag from 2 to 8 preserves stability and accuracy. With Qwen3-30B-A3B and Python tools, macro pass@1 improves from 31.29% to 71.55%. On OSWorld, Nemotron-3-Nano-Omni-30B’s accuracy improves from 50.97% to 56.16%, with training-step time only 6.8% above the standard-kernel baseline.

We introduce Mistral Large 4 (ML4), a 52B active, 1T total parameter multimodal mixture-of-experts model designed for reasoning and long-horizon agentic tasks. We build a scalable agent-based pipeline that authors and verifies executable environments for software engineering, cybersecurity, and knowledge work. Mistral Large 4 achieves competitive performance on code, cybersecurity, and held-out agentic benchmarks, including 19.7% on FrontierCode 2.0, 41% on Terminal-Bench 4.0, and 50.9% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index. Efficient serving combines sparse attention, optimized context parallelism, prefill–decode disaggregation, and speculative decoding. Calibrated NVFP4 quantization reduces the checkpoint to 606 GB while matching the FP8 reference on evaluations, enabling deployment on four GB300 GPUs. Multiple-teacher distillation provides high, medium, and low reasoning-effort modes, allowing users to control the trade-off between token consumption and performance.

Coding agents working in shared repositories may receive separate, independently-motivated requests from human developers, creating a setting that is multi-agent by necessity. When this scenario happens, their individual implementations may work separately but conflict when combined. To study this setting, we introduce ParallACT, a benchmark of orchestrator-free multi-agent coding tasks. ParallACT contains both complementary and contradictory tasks. In complementary tasks, each agent's task is separately useful and implementations must share an interface to be productively combined. In contradictory pairs, both agents' tasks require editing the same code in incompatible ways, and naively combining independent solutions fails to produce a useful implementation. We compare a single-agent oracle given the combined set of tasks against multi-agent settings that vary execution order, visibility, awareness of other agents, and access to a communication channel. We find that the oracle solves most tasks while parallel agents perform substantially worse. Their performance drop is notable for complementary tasks, and particularly sharp for contradictory tasks (e.g., from 62% to 16% for Claude Code with Claude Opus 4.8) where merged code typically satisfies only one specification, and the same gap appears in all six further configurations pairing two agent harnesses with three open-weight models. Simply telling an agent that a peer exists does not help significantly, and giving agents access to a communication channel recovers only a small part of the performance, at an additional token cost. ParallACT thus identifies and isolates a core challenge that will become more common as multi-agent coding by independent principals becomes standard, and provides a controlled test of which coordination strategies help, and at what cost.

We introduce SIMIT, a test-time self-improvement framework in which a vision-language model creates its own query-specific training data before answering an unlabeled test query. Our goal is to improve performance on a given target test set without annotations or external models. To pursue this goal, some test-time methods improve answers through longer reasoning or repeated sampling but leave the model unchanged. Others update the model using rewards based on majority agreement among multiple candidate answers or the model's own judgments of correctness, but such rewards can reinforce existing mistakes. SIMIT instead imagines similar problems whose solutions it controls: a model need not correctly solve the target query to construct useful practice examples. It synthesizes diverse (question, answer, image) triplets by specifying each answer before realizing its image. To support diverse multimodal tasks, SIMIT combines native image generation with an extensible skill library for structured visuals, including documents, charts, and diagrams. Within this pipeline, multi-stage verification checks that images support their assigned answers, while difficulty filtering retains informative examples. Adaptive budgeting further targets this practice by allocating more samples to queries the model is less confident in answering. The resulting data can improve the model in-context (SIMIT-ICL) or in-weight (SIMIT-FT). Across 17 diverse benchmarks, SIMIT outperforms existing self-improvement methods. Its best configuration achieves a +7.20% mean relative gain over BAGEL-7B, while training-free SIMIT-ICL achieves +6.98%.

Short convolution has become a common local mixing component in modern sequence models, yet existing variants are typically static: a single learned kernel defines the same local aggregation rule at every position. We introduce Mixture of Convolutions (MoC), a simple adaptive generalization of short convolution that replaces this single kernel with a mixture over learned convolutional bases. Evaluated in both Transformer and Gated DeltaNet architectures, MoC shows broad improvements in language-modeling perplexity over static short convolution, at modest additional cost. We additionally study how short convolutions are optimized, and find that their performance is sensitive to the interaction between initialization scale and learning rate, in a way that affects static short convolution as well as MoC. These results suggest that token-adaptive local mixing is a simple and effective extension of a widely used sequence-modeling primitive.

Accelerating modern foundational models has pushed domain-specific compilers toward increasingly complex, multi-tiered optimization pipelines. However, this heavy optimization focus introduces delicate tradeoffs between peak execution performance and correctness. Subtle codegen defects can trigger numerical degradation and memory or buffer corruption, invalidating multi-million-dollar training runs and degrading live serving quality without raising obvious compiler errors. In this paper, we present a battle-tested methodology for verifying and triaging Google's XLA:TPU compiler at hyperscale. We leverage fuzzing techniques, combining synthetic program generation with real production traces, while orchestrating AI agent swarms to autonomously generate stress tests, reproduce failures, and draft fixes. To pinpoint root causes in full workloads, we pair this with a hierarchical differential pipeline that bisects large graphs down to individual failing operations inside fused kernels. Deployed in production, our framework has already driven the resolution of over 142 compiler bugs (with 103 additional findings under review), from which we distill pragmatic lessons learned.

Deploying generative world models for end-to-end closed-loop evaluation and policy learning requires precise scenario control, consistent observations, and sustained generation quality during extended interactions. This report presents X-World 1.6, advancing X-World 1.0 toward a more reliable and versatile driving simulator. The upgraded base model offers finer-grained control over traffic semantics, including traffic lights and road markings, together with improved spatial consistency across cameras. Virtual City capabilities broaden scenario construction through a family of models conditioned on diverse 2D and 3D references, including support for generating multi-camera future videos from a single image. An enhanced post-training framework enables efficient causal, few-step generation with stronger temporal coherence, better quality retention over longer rollouts, and improved alignment with human preferences. We also introduce a dedicated evaluation suite to support systematic assessment and guide model iteration. Together, these upgrades expand the scenarios X-World can simulate and improve the efficiency and reliability of its generated observations, supporting broader use in autonomous-driving development.

Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) encode relative position by rotating pairs of query and key coordinates according to token position. However, these pairs already have content-dependent orientations before the positional rotation is applied, so content-dependent orientation and positional phase interact within the same angular term of the attention score. We introduce Rotary Orientation Contraction (ROC), a simple modification to RoPE that learns how strongly to contract these pre-existing orientations while preserving the standard RoPE frequencies and positional rotations. Across language-modeling experiments with QK normalization, ROC improves perplexity over matched RoPE baselines and achieves higher average accuracy on downstream benchmarks at both evaluated model scales. These results identify pre-RoPE content geometry as a useful design dimension for rotary attention and show that it can be modified efficiently, with essentially no measured forward-pass overhead, while preserving the standard paired RoPE structure.

Large language model (LLM) agents extend their capabilities with skills, each with a name, a description, and a body. Under progressive disclosure, an LLM router selects skills by name and description alone and loads only the selected bodies. Skill libraries grow continually as users and agents add new skills. Because the router relies on this metadata, a similar new skill can displace an earlier one, breaking previously correct routing even though the earlier skill and the router are unchanged. This routing interference is aggravated for public skills, whose descriptions may not match their bodies. We formulate the problem as lifelong skill routing, a class-incremental continual learning problem. A solution must keep earlier skills selectable without suppressing new ones. Existing approaches fall short, since continually retraining the router risks catastrophic forgetting and rewriting methods either ignore similar skills or require per-skill feedback. We therefore propose Skill++, which rewrites only the name and description of each incoming skill, without router training or labeled data. The new description states what the body supports, how the skill differs from its closest predecessor, and what related work it excludes. As a library grows to 731 skills over ten sessions, Skill++ selects all required skills for 76.3% of queries, versus 36.4% under the original metadata. Across three benchmarks and five LLM routers, it outperforms all compared approaches, and its gains carry over to the Codex CLI agent harness.

We present WeSearch, a unified, model-centric retrieval framework for large-scale, continuously evolving content search. Prevailing methods assign documents fixed hierarchical Semantic IDs, implicitly assuming each document follows a single coherent semantic path-an assumption that often breaks down for multi-topic documents. WeSearch instead retrieves query-relevant clusters and then ranks atomic documents within the resulting query-specific candidate space, decoupling candidate pruning from fine-grained relevance modeling. Combined with relevance-aware training, compact document representations, and incremental index updates, this design enables weekly-or daily when needed-model refreshes. Deployed as the primary semantic retrieval path in WeChat Search alongside a lexical syntax tree, WeSearch shows consistent one-week A/B gains on corpora from hundreds of millions to billions of documents, and a one-month full-traffic A/B test confirms stable improvements of +0.68% CTR and +2.27% per-user article clicks, together with a 41% reduction in retrieval resource cost and a 19 ms reduction in graphic-text retrieval latency. WeSearch is now fully deployed in WeChat Search, serving 100% of production traffic.

LLMs degrade in multi-turn conversation partly because of context pollution: the model's own earlier outputs stay in context and anchor later turns, so an early misreading of the user's intent can persist after the user corrects it. Assistant omission (AO), dropping every assistant message, removes this pollution but fails when interaction is referential: later turns refer back to drafts, decisions, and tool-call results that exist only in assistant turns. We propose Agentic Conversation Context Curation (AC3), a training-free method in which a separate analyzer (1) consolidates the task specification from the user's messages alone, (2) audits the assistant's prior outputs against it, and (3) edits the context, either appending the analysis or discarding the assistant side and rebuilding the context from the specification. A second finding: pollution is contagious. An analyzer that sees the assistant's reasoning while extracting the specification can do worse than no intervention, and instructing it to ignore them did not close the gap, so we exclude assistant turns structurally. On Lost in Conversation (replaying difficulty-selected instances), where AO is an oracle by construction, AC3 closes 55-84% of the gap between full context and AO on three of four tasks and exceeds AO on the fourth, and an LLM that faithfully summarizes the history does not reproduce the gain even with more compute. On real WildChat conversations, a GPT-5-mini judge prefers AC3's next turn over both full context and AO in every configuration of our main table, though this preference depends on the judge; on CollabLLM results are mixed. In stateful tool use (tau2-bench), AO collapses to 0% on every model; AC3 does not collapse, though it falls slightly behind full context. Detector studies show that Reset removes injected pollution but is not span-selective: the gain comes from rebuilding the specification.
